identity.title: Controlling Underestimation Bias in Constrained Reinforcement Learning for Safe Exploration

problem.claim: Constrained reinforcement learning seeks to maximize cumulative reward while satisfying constraints.

gap.claim: Existing CRL algorithms often incur substantial training-time constraint violations; the authors identify cost-value underestimation as a contributing factor.

contributions.claim: MICE introduces intrinsic costs based on remembered unsafe states and applies bias control to mitigate cost-value underestimation during exploration.
An extrinsic-intrinsic cost value function combines intrinsic costs with a bias-correction strategy and supports a trust-region optimization objective with corresponding optimization methods.
The paper reports convergence guarantees for the proposed cost value function and a worst-case constraint-violation result for the MICE update.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish MICE through memory-driven unsafe-state identification, pseudo-count intrinsic costs, and bias-corrected extrinsic-intrinsic cost estimation.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that extensive experiments significantly reduce constraint violations while preserving policy performance comparable to baselines.
The authors report convergence guarantees for the proposed cost value function and establish the worst-case constraint violation for the MICE update.

narrative_sequence.summary: CRL balances reward maximization with constraint satisfaction, but existing methods often violate constraints during training.
The paper attributes these violations in part to underestimation of the cost value function.
MICE remembers previously explored unsafe states, identifies high-cost regions, assigns pseudo-count intrinsic costs, and uses bias-corrected cost estimation.
The paper reports trust-region optimization methods, theoretical guarantees, and experiments showing fewer violations with baseline-comparable policy performance.

source_observation.claim: The abstract links a concrete failure mode—cost-value underestimation—to a targeted mechanism that remembers unsafe states and adds intrinsic costs.

lessons.interpretation: A method narrative is more diagnostically useful when it maps an identified error source to an explicit intervention.
lessons.application: Frame a safety-oriented contribution as failure mode → measurable surrogate or memory signal → corrected objective, and preserve that mapping in the abstract.
lessons.exception: This framing is unsuitable when the failure mode is not empirically or theoretically tied to the proposed intervention.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify environments, violation metrics, baseline identities, or experimental conditions behind the reported comparison.
The assumptions for the convergence and worst-case violation claims are not stated.
The abstract does not quantify the reported reduction in violations or define what policy performance is preserved.
